newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo NBY cuts discount rate amidst high insolvency.
newsitem.headline: Yugo NBY cuts discount rate amidst high insolvency.

text.p: The National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) said on Wednesday it had cut its key discount rate for March to 2.5 percent per month from 4.5 percent in February.
But analysts said it would not have any significant impact on the business of companies and banks.
At an annual level it dropped to 33.74 percent from 77.5 percent in the previous month.
This was the second change of the NBY discount rate since last June when it was cut to 4.5 percent from 6.31 percent in May.
"We have decided to cut the discount rate this month following a low increase in retail prices," acting managing director of the NBY monetary policy department Pavao Marjanovic told Reuters.
Retail prices in February were only 0.6 percent up against January when they rose 1.4 percent against the previous month.
"One of the main economic policy goals is stability of currency and prices and our monetary policy will be as restrictive as needed to ensure that," Marjanovic said.
The discount rate was said to be the NBY's key instrument in regulating market liquidity.
Marjanovic said the NBY sopped up about 300 million dinars in the past two months after strong monetary expansion at the end of 1996 and the plunge in the dinar black market rate.
"The NBY has almost brought the money supply M1 to the December level, restoring dinar's stability," he said.
Money supply M1 at the end of February stood at about 5.54 billion dinars compared to 5.49 billion last December, he said.
Analysts were doubtful about the effect of the lower discount rate because of the existing lack of capital.
"Cutting the discount rate alone cannot improve business as most funds are completely exhausted," said one analyst who asked not to be named.

The best proof of the current insolvency in the entire economy is that the currency black market street dealers are selling the German mark for 3.8 dinars which is a slight drop from 3.9 dinars last week, another analyst said.
The official exchange rate is 3.3 dinars to the mark.
"There are thousands of German marks on the streets but no dinars and the black market rate could easily decline further," the analyst said.

NBY sets its discount rate each month using a basket that includes interest rates on the open money market and its short-term bonds, price rises, expected monetary developments, credit demand and money supply.
